Rebalancing while taking money out: choose the sale source before adding another trade

Four charts compare proportional and target-directed withdrawals, showing the cash taken out, the remaining asset weights and any separate exchange still needed.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two sources for the same pre-tax portfolio withdrawal

Interactive planning lab

Cash withdrawn, before tax and costs$30,000
Directed withdrawal: equity share remaining66.67%
Requested withdrawal left unfunded$0

Hypothetical two-asset portfolio with one immediate withdrawal, no price movement, tax, fees, settlement delay or account restriction. A proportional withdrawal sells each asset in its starting weight. The directed rule chooses a feasible equity sale that minimizes distance to the entered target after taking the same cash out; it cannot sell extra assets and reinvest proceeds. Requested cash is capped at total assets and any unfunded remainder is reported. A fully spent portfolio has no remaining allocation. The chosen target is a reader assumption, not a recommended risk level or a forecast.

The central idea

A withdrawal can move an allocation toward a target, but the target applies to the smaller portfolio left behind. Taking cash out does not always complete the rebalance.

01

Ask where the same withdrawal will come from

Two portfolios can begin with the same holdings, provide the same spending cash and finish with different asset weights. The difference can come entirely from the choice of assets sold, even before any market movement.

Investor.gov defines rebalancing as bringing a portfolio back toward its original allocation. This article considers a related cash-flow question: when money already needs to leave, how much of that allocation adjustment can the required sale accomplish?

The example has only equity and bond buckets. It does not select securities or judge the entered target’s suitability. The SEC’s allocation guide places asset mix in the context of investment horizon and risk tolerance. A mechanically achievable percentage is not automatically the right percentage for a household.

02

Reconcile the starting holdings and the cash leaving

The default portfolio is CAD 300,000 with 70% in equity and 30% in bonds. That means CAD 210,000 of equity and CAD 90,000 of bonds. The requested withdrawal is CAD 30,000 before tax and transaction costs.

Both illustrated rules supply exactly that CAD 30,000. Both leave a CAD 270,000 investment portfolio. The first stacked comparison therefore has the same ending total under either rule, making it possible to inspect composition without confusing it with a difference in wealth.

The cash withdrawn is outside the remaining portfolio. It is not shown as another investment asset, and no return is applied to it. The tool also does not claim that a gross withdrawal is the same as a household’s after-tax spending amount.

03

A proportional sale preserves the existing weight

The proportional rule uses the starting 70/30 mix to fund the withdrawal. It sells CAD 21,000 of equity and CAD 9,000 of bonds, leaving CAD 189,000 and CAD 81,000 respectively.

CAD 189,000 divided by CAD 270,000 is still 70%. Selling both buckets in proportion does not by itself correct the original allocation drift. It simply scales the portfolio down under the model’s no-price-change assumptions.

This is a useful control case. If a proposed withdrawal strategy claims to change risk exposure, check the weights of what remains rather than the percentage of the withdrawal that came from each asset. Those are different denominators.

04

Apply the target to the portfolio remaining after the withdrawal

The entered target is 60% equity. After CAD 30,000 leaves, that target would mean CAD 162,000 of equity in the CAD 270,000 remaining portfolio. Starting from CAD 210,000, reaching it would require CAD 48,000 of equity sales.

The spending withdrawal is only CAD 30,000. The directed rule is not allowed to sell CAD 48,000 and silently reinvest CAD 18,000 in bonds. It can sell only enough assets to provide the requested spending cash.

It therefore takes all CAD 30,000 from equity in the default example. The remaining holdings are CAD 180,000 of equity and CAD 90,000 of bonds. Equity falls to about 66.67%: closer to 60%, but not at the target.

05

Make the extra exchange visible rather than hiding it inside the withdrawal

The default directed portfolio still has CAD 18,000 more equity than the 60% target permits. Reaching the target would require a separate exchange: sell another CAD 18,000 of equity and buy CAD 18,000 of bonds. That exchange is not executed in the model.

The matrix reports this residual in dollars. Positive means equity still above target; negative means equity below target. A negative cell would require an equity purchase, funded by an equal bond reduction, if the target were to be reached with a separate trade.

Rows replace the target equity percentage. Columns replace the withdrawal with a percentage of starting assets. The original equity weight remains selected. This lets the reader see when a cash withdrawal can finish the adjustment and when it cannot.

06

Respect the assets available and the amount actually needed

The directed rule cannot sell a negative amount or more than the holding available. Within those limits, it chooses the source split closest to the entered equity target after funding the withdrawal. It does not use leverage or buy an asset during the spending transaction.

With a CAD 75,000 withdrawal under the default starting mix, taking all of it from equity leaves CAD 135,000 of equity and CAD 90,000 of bonds, exactly a 60/40 mix. A larger withdrawal can require sales from both buckets. If the entire portfolio is spent, there is no remaining allocation to measure.

Requests above available assets are capped, with the unfunded amount displayed separately. Tax, dealing charges, spreads, settlement dates, registered-account rules and future market changes need another layer of planning. The charts compare sale sources for a single hypothetical transaction; they do not establish a withdrawal order that is best for every account.
